text: In flight: 24-h systolic pressure was about 8 mmHg lower than before flight (8 ISS astronauts, 85-192 days).
In flight: 24-h diastolic pressure was about 9 mmHg lower than before flight (8 ISS astronauts).
In flight: heart rate did not change compared with before flight, while the heart pumped about 35% more blood per beat (8 ISS astronauts).
In flight: astronauts slept 6.09 h a night on average on the ISS, against 8.5 h scheduled (21 ISS astronauts).
Without gravity, bone and muscle are lost; daily exercise is the main countermeasure.
Isolation and confinement are one of NASA's five spaceflight hazards and affect mood, sleep and team work.

NASA lists behavioral changes and psychiatric disorders (risk 12) among the effects of isolation, confinement and distance. Canada's C-STARS study tracks stress and coping with questionnaires and diary entries during the mission.
NASA risk 14 names sleep loss, circadian desynchronization and work overload together as causes of performance decrements and adverse health outcomes.

NASA: mild hypoxia can cause confusion, headaches, vision impairment and trouble sleeping (risk 6). Cabin CO2 at levels nobody notices in a day causes headaches and irritability after months (Hazard 5 podcast).
NASA: some ISS astronauts have reported cold sores, rashes, atypical allergies and infections that can be attributed to immune system alterations (risk 1).
NASA: the majority of astronauts experience motion sickness during spaceflight; changes in gravity affect orientation, coordination and balance (risk 2).
NASA: approximately 70 percent of ISS astronauts experience some swelling in the back of their eyes (SANS, risk 10). Canada's SANSORI study reports the same figure.
